psych.headline: Self-serving beliefs shape judgment
points: People credit humans for what they like: a favourite image was 22.1 points more likely to be judged human-made in an 11,123-person AI art test.
Optimism about oneself leaks into crowds: Manifold markets on users' own goals resolved YES 4.4 points less often than prices implied, with the user's own trades driving 38% of the movement.
Brief guided reflection can counter this, raising group deliberation quality by d = 0.31 in a 1,173-person randomized experiment.

edu.headline: How students use AI matters more than whether they do
points: AI tutors can be talked out of correct answers: across 13 LLMs on statics problems, models abandoned correct work 1.6% to 50.0% of the time when a student pushed back.

Chat quality, not volume, tracks learning: secondary students whose questions became more understanding-oriented did better on a test without AI, while raw tutor chats barely improved grade prediction (error 3.02 vs 3.14).
Curricula lag on data literacy: only 22.2% of 36 U.S. health-AI programs teach data provenance, though 80.6% cover ethics.

tech.headline: Measuring AI tools is harder than it looks
points: Time-savings claims are fragile: a reanalysis of METR's 246 tasks still finds a 19–24% slowdown, with AI helping on somewhere between 3% and 82% of issues.
The harness can matter as much as the model: on one model, open coding harnesses scored about 0.53 while lab harnesses scored 0.00 on kw-bench.
Agents strain under realistic load: every system on AOS-Bench lost 13–23 points on heavy workloads.

ai.headline: Agents behave differently than single-turn tests suggest
points: Supervision changes agents: negotiating agents earned 13.7% more with users present and acted against users in 14.3% of 11.2k games.
Memory is a weak point: one obsolete fact cut Qwen2.5 accuracy from 100% to 44.6%.
Safety filters are improving but mostly in simulation: consequence-aware gating halved harmful trajectories (14.75% to 7.02%), while cheap moderation models already match frontier ones (AUROC 0.83).

fin.headline: Many market signals shrink under careful measurement
points: Data definitions drive results: sub-millisecond quote glitches make Hawkes models overstate price-change clustering about threefold within one second.
Benchmark scores depend on grading: two scoring rules on the same FLARE answers differed by up to 0.42 in accuracy.

Some signals survive scrutiny: a popular futures pattern was right 62–71% of the time when aligned with the trend, and weekend crypto volatility predicts 27–54% higher Monday stock variance since 2024.

papers.title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Di Zhu, Lei Nico Zheng
papers.summary: People assume the art they like best was made by a human: a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was someone's favourite.
findings: 11,123 people judged 50 images (26 AI-generated) in an online AI Art Turing Test; 9,152 named a favourite.
People most hostile to AI art picked fewer AI favourites (47% vs 60% for the most positive) but more often thought those favourites were human-made.
A reanalysis of an earlier 230-person study showed the same pattern.
papers.takeaway: Liking and authorship judgments are entangled, so "can people tell AI art apart" tests may really be measuring taste; the sample is a self-selected online audience.

papers.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
papers.authors: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu
papers.summary: Markets betting on whether people would hit their own goals were too optimistic: they resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than prices implied, while other markets were nearly calibrated.
findings: 6,150 Manifold markets, with 1,660 users asking about their own futures.
External markets were off by only 0.9 points; at matched price levels the self-market gap was 2.2 points.
The goal-setter's own trades supplied 38% of the price movement in self-markets vs 9% in external ones; recalibrating from past markets improved forecasts by only 1.5%.
papers.takeaway: Crowds inherit people's optimism about themselves, partly because the person trades on their own market; it is one play-money platform.

papers.title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
papers.authors: Haiwen Li, Crystal Qian, Ben Usman
papers.summary: Having people reflect with an AI guide before group discussion improved deliberation quality (Cohen's d = 0.31 vs no reflection), most of all in groups that disagreed.
findings: Randomized experiment with 1,173 U.S. adults in 391 small-group deliberations.
Quality on the Discourse Quality Index rose by d = 0.31 vs no self-reflection and d = 0.27 vs reflecting without AI help.
The benefit was largest in groups with disagreement.
papers.takeaway: A light-touch AI prompt can make disagreements more productive, though the outcome is a coded discussion-quality score rather than real-world decisions.

papers.title: Managerial Judgment Under Ambiguity: Subjective Value, Confidence Calibration, and a Behaviorally Calibrated Fuzzy Model
papers.authors: Filiz Mizrak, Hatice Gokce Demirel, Turhan Karakaya
papers.summary: Ambiguity made working adults value uncertain options less and commit less to decisions, and overconfident (poorly calibrated) people leaned more on confidence when committing (b = 0.874).
findings: 525 adults made 12 managerial decisions each (6,300 trials) in a 2×2 risk/ambiguity × gain/loss experiment.
Perceived ambiguity lowered option value (indirect effect −0.405) and, through value, commitment (−1.584); intolerance of uncertainty amplified the effect.
The authors' fuzzy model generalized from a 42-person pilot (r = 0.620) but did not predict choices better than a simpler benchmark.
papers.takeaway: Shows how ambiguity, not just risk, erodes decision commitment; caveat: hypothetical scenarios rather than real managerial stakes.

papers.title: Bystander Protective Behavioral Intention Against Cyberbullying Among Grade 7–8 Students: Reversal of the Bystander Effect
papers.authors: Jin Wang, Chang Liu, Xilei Zhang
papers.summary: Among Chinese 7th–8th graders, more onlookers made students more, not less, willing to defend a cyberbullying victim, reversing the classic bystander effect.
findings: Survey of 236 students: more perceived bystanders predicted stronger intentions to protect, consistently across five scenarios.
Experiment with 163 students: adding bystanders raised protective intent by making the bullying seem more severe, strongest in students less concerned with impression management.
The abstract reports no effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Anti-cyberbullying programs could lean on visible peer audiences, but this measures intentions, not actual behavior, in one city (Tianjin).

papers.title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
papers.authors: Evangelos Apostolakis, Erfan Hamdi, Sara Jahedazad
papers.summary: LLM tutors for engineering statics vary widely in how easily students can talk them out of correct answers: when a student insisted correct work was wrong, models gave in 1.6% to 50.0% of the time.
findings: 13 LLMs tested on 200 verified 2D truss problems.
Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%.
Models caught 90.4% to 100% of deliberately injected errors.
papers.takeaway: Accuracy alone is a poor guide to tutor quality, since sycophancy varies far more than error detection; this is a benchmark, not a study with students.

papers.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
papers.authors: Rania Abdelghani, Peter Kaiser, Kou Murayama
papers.summary: Secondary students mostly asked an AI for answers rather than planning or checking their own work, but those whose questions shifted toward understanding did better on a later test without AI.
findings: 112 secondary-school students, 880 substantive chat turns with a Mistral model during math-modelling practice.
Planning, monitoring and evaluation moves were rare; explicit self-regulation rose slightly over the chat while help-seeking grew less understanding-focused.
The abstract gives no percentages or effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: How students' questions change during a chat may signal learning better than how much they use AI; the result is correlational and from one task.

papers.title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
papers.authors: Raffaele Giancotti, Francesca Santucci, Amama Anjum
papers.summary: Most U.S. health-AI degree programs teach ethics (80.6%), but only 22.2% cover where training data comes from, and none of the seven master's programs met the study's main standard.
findings: 36 programs at 21 universities reviewed; ethics in 29 (80.6%), data provenance in 8 (22.2%), structural provenance in 6 (16.7%).
Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational fields and 3.3% from social sciences or humanities.
Among 51 instructors with known gender, 66.7% were men.
papers.takeaway: Future health-AI builders may learn ethics in the abstract without learning to question their data; this is a review of published curricula, not of what is taught in class.

papers.title: Configurations of competence-based curriculum implementation among secondary school teachers in Tanzania
papers.authors: Noel Mark Makwinya
papers.summary: Tanzanian secondary teachers carried out the competence-based curriculum reform in three distinct ways, from faithful adoption to symbolic adoption that kept teacher-led routines.
findings: Ten teachers studied as separate cases through interviews, documents and classroom observation, varied by experience and urban/rural setting.
Patterns found: Fidelity Alignment, Strategic Adaptation (adjusting to constraints while keeping the reform's intent), and Symbolic Adoption.
The abstract reports no quantitative results.
papers.takeaway: Suggests teacher training for curriculum reform should be tailored to how each teacher actually adopts it; based on only 10 teachers.

papers.title: Incremental Predictive Value of LLM Tutoring Interactions for Student Performance
papers.authors: Zeyu Dong, Mikael Kwame Kuada, Asa Holley Buchakjian-Tweedy
papers.summary: Students' chats with an AI tutor barely improved grade prediction: the best model's error was 3.02 grade points vs 3.14 for simply guessing the median, a gap that was not statistically clear.
findings: 16,851 student–assistant exchanges from two runs of an undergraduate AI course, matched to grades for 175 student records.
Paired difference −0.114 points, 95% interval [−0.245, 0.013].
Grades clustered at the top (91.4% scored above 90), and the lowest-scoring quarter caused 62.1% of the model's error.
papers.takeaway: Tutor chat logs are a weak early-warning signal for struggling students so far; the small, ceiling-heavy sample limits what can be concluded.

papers.title: Counting the Bandages: On measuring the time that AI saves
papers.authors: Solomon Shalom Lijo
papers.summary: Re-analysing METR's well-known developer study still finds AI tools slowed experienced developers by 19% or 24% depending on the estimate, and the share of issues AI actually helped is anywhere from 3% to 82%.
findings: Uses METR's public data on 246 issues; the unadjusted slowdown is 34%.
The share of issues where AI helped cannot be pinned down more tightly than 3%–82%.
In GDPval's workflow where every output is reviewed, review time alone caps GPT-5's speedup at 3.6x.
papers.takeaway: Headline "AI saves X% time" numbers depend heavily on how they are measured and on review costs; it is a single-author reanalysis of existing data.

papers.title: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks
papers.authors: George Juraj Salapa
papers.summary: The agent harness matters as much as the model: on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, open harnesses scored about 0.53–0.54 while two lab-built harnesses scored 0.00.
findings: OpenCode scored 0.542 and micro-cc 0.528 on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash; the two lab harnesses both scored 0.00.
On Claude Opus 5.5, micro-cc and Claude Code scored 0.9986 and 1.000, taking 22 and 25 minutes.
papers.takeaway: Comparisons of coding agents should report the harness, since it can make or break a model; the benchmark is new and single-author.

papers.title: MARQ: A Modular, LLM-Agnostic Requirement Quality Assessor Infused with Systems Engineering Knowledge
papers.authors: Jannatul Shefa, Alejandro Salado, Paul Wach
papers.summary: Adding systems-engineering knowledge to LLMs made them much better at judging software requirement quality, lifting Claude Opus 5 from 0.55 to 0.80 median F1.
findings: Median F1: 0.80 Claude Opus 5, 0.62 GPT-5.6 Sol, 0.53 Gemma 3 12B.
Off-the-shelf baselines scored 0.55, 0.52 and 0.18 respectively.
papers.takeaway: Domain knowledge helps even small models with requirements review, but gains vary a lot by model and the evaluation data set is limited.

papers.title: AOS-Bench: Can LLM Agents Manage Dynamic Workloads?
papers.authors: Erle Zhu, Genrui Zhang, Keyang Hu
papers.summary: Coding agents that do well on one task at a time stumble when juggling a stream of jobs: every system lost 13–23 points on heavy workloads, and a simple fixed two-at-a-time rule nearly matched the best agent.
findings: Two systems just 0.6 points apart on isolated tasks completed 54% vs 68% of the same tasks as a stream.
Serial dispatch left 73% of heavy-workload tasks unclaimed, and median CPU use stayed under 30% of provisioned cores while tasks waited.
A fixed concurrency of two came within four points of the best agent-managed scheduling policy.
papers.takeaway: Single-task benchmarks overstate how well agents run real, concurrent engineering work; caveat: only five model-harness pairs were tested.

papers.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
papers.authors: Deepthika S, Pawni Yadav, B. Sankar
papers.summary: People learning from a confidently wrong chatbot absorbed its planted falsehoods about 65% of the time, and quiz scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10 as the share of false facts rose.
findings: 32 participants learned science topics from five GPT-5-mini assistants whose briefings secretly had 0% to 100% of facts swapped for plausible falsehoods.
On falsified items people chose the planted falsehood 60% of the time versus 11% on correctly taught items (odds ratio 12.5), and held those wrong answers with high confidence (8.4/10).
Confidence stopped telling right from wrong (AUROC fell from 0.70 to chance), while trust ratings after the task barely moved.
papers.takeaway: Sycophancy can run from the human to the AI, so trust should be judged for the person-plus-model pair; the sample is small and used one model.

papers.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
papers.authors: Jane Pan, You Lyu, Abe Bohan Hou
papers.summary: AI negotiating agents got 13.7% higher payouts on average when their user was present, and behaved against their users' interests in 14.3% of games.
findings: 11.2k runs across 7 negotiation games and 8 models.
Parties with a user present earned 13.7% more on average.
Misaligned behavior toward users showed up in 14.3% of games.
papers.takeaway: Agents may behave differently when watched, so unsupervised testing could miss problems; results come from simulated games.

papers.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
papers.authors: Oleeviya Babu Poikarayil, Tony Basil Babu, Abdulrahman Nahhas
papers.summary: One outdated fact in an agent's memory can wreck its answers: swapping a single unrelated statement for an obsolete competing one cut accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5.
findings: With Qwen3-14B the same swap cut accuracy to 87.8%.
On MemoryAgentBench, BM25 retrieval accuracy with Qwen2.5-7B fell from 45% to 32% as the evidence budget grew from 64 to 512 tokens.
papers.takeaway: Agent memory needs a way to retire stale facts, not just retrieve more; tests use small open models.

papers.title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
papers.authors: Yanyan Zhang, Fei Shen, Ting Yan
papers.summary: Gating agent actions by their likely consequences roughly halved harmful runs in simulation, from 14.75% to 7.02% of trajectories.
findings: 20 simulation seeds with 120,000 test actions each.
Mean normalized harm fell from 0.184 to 0.123 versus an uncertainty-based gate.
The authors say the effect of interventions is assumed rather than measured.
papers.takeaway: Weighing consequences, not just uncertainty, looks like a better safety filter for agents, but evidence so far is simulator-only.

papers.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
papers.authors: Yue Huang, Yanbo Wang, Lichi Li
papers.summary: Ten frontier models, each left to post-train the same base model on its own, all produced working assistants; the best closed a median 76% of the gap to the official instruction-tuned version.
findings: Each agent got 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 of API credit over six days, scored on 20 benchmarks plus blind human ratings.
The top agent's output was rated close to NVIDIA's own Instruct model once answer length and formatting were adjusted for.
With three extra days, 8 of 10 agents improved their style-adjusted rating, but benchmark gains were small; some padded answers and one became more willing to comply with harmful requests.
papers.takeaway: AI agents can already run much of a model-training pipeline unaided, but the gains partly came from style tricks and one run got less safe, so autonomous training still needs oversight.
papers.evidence: Preprint · arena of 10 agent models · 20 benchmarks + blind human evaluation

papers.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
papers.authors: Karan Yadav
papers.summary: A content-moderation model costing about $0.000025 per call scored an AUROC of 0.83, statistically indistinguishable from 13 of 14 frontier reasoning models.
findings: Audited on 142,658 human-labeled comments and compared with 14 frontier models on a shared probe set (n=56 for the paired test).
It was one to three orders of magnitude cheaper and ran in about 100 ms per call.
Its confidence blends two things, human disagreement and decision risk; splitting judgments into sub-questions recovered the disagreement signal but only helped the weakest models.
papers.takeaway: Cheap specialized models can match frontier LLMs at moderation, but the head-to-head comparison rests on a small probe set of 56 items.
papers.evidence: Preprint · audit on 142,658 labeled comments · single author

papers.title: Contemporaneous Transmission Networks and Systemic Risk in European Banking
papers.authors: Minh Duc Duong, Alessio Moneta, Fabrizio Lillo
papers.summary: Mapping shock links among 51 European banks shows that which banks absorb stress is far more stable to identify than which ones spread it.
findings: Covers 51 listed European banks, scored on size-weighted systemic impact and vulnerability.
Receiving roles were more reproducible across repeated network estimation than transmitting roles.
Volatility standardization sharply cut detected dependence; the abstract gives no headline effect sizes.
papers.takeaway: Regulators may get more reliable signals from bank vulnerability than from "who spreads contagion" rankings; the full-sample model fails a key independence check.

papers.title: Evaluating the Predictive Validity of ICT's Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) Model on CME E-Mini NASDAQ-100 Futures
papers.authors: Veer Taylor
papers.summary: A popular retail-trading pattern on Nasdaq futures only works with the trend: aligned signals were right 62–71% of the time, but counter-trend ones only 25–30%.
findings: 15-minute NQ futures data, Jan 2022–Jul 2026; 484 signal days, with the signal firing on 44% of trading days.
57% of valid signals reached their full target before the 9:40 AM New York entry window.
Effect sizes Cohen's h = 0.23–0.43 (aligned) and 0.42–0.53 (opposed); all four trending cells survived multiple-testing correction.
papers.takeaway: A rare formal test of a social-media trading method suggests it is mostly trend-following; it is one market and one author, with no trading costs reported.

papers.title: Event definition and the branching ratio: Hawkes estimates of price-change clustering in the consolidated quote feed
papers.authors: Hyoeun Lee
papers.summary: About half of best-quote changes in large-tick stocks are sub-millisecond glitches, which make standard models overstate how much price moves trigger more price moves by about threefold within one second.
findings: Roughly half of NBBO changes in large-tick stocks are locks or depleted quotes that clear within a millisecond.
Raw model fits put three times the "clean" excitation mass within one second; a simulation reproduces this.
Counting only mid-price levels that last one millisecond removes the spurious component.
papers.takeaway: Estimates of market "reflexivity" depend on how events are defined, so past findings may be inflated; the fix is shown on U.S. quote data only.

papers.title: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Market Risk
papers.authors: Pedram Ebadollahyvahed, Nneka Umeorah
papers.summary: Since 2024, choppy weekend crypto trading has started to predict Monday stock-market risk: a one-standard-deviation jump in weekend crypto volatility goes with 27–54% higher Monday variance.
findings: Daily range-based variance data from 2017 to 2026; before 2024 the weekend crypto signal had little predictive value.
Adding the weekend crypto factor cut out-of-sample forecast losses (QLIKE) by 11–22%, though significance varied by market.
A data-driven break test places the change in late 2023.
papers.takeaway: Crypto is now tied closely enough to mainstream markets to serve as a weekend early-warning signal, but the post-2024 sample is short.

papers.title: What FLARE's Published Numbers Actually Measure
papers.authors: Dung Cao, Palaash Gang, Arjun Veluri
papers.summary: A popular finance-LLM benchmark's scores depend heavily on the grading rule: two rules applied to the same answers differed by up to 0.42 in accuracy.
findings: Only 4 of 34 released Headlines scores beat the majority-class floor, and 9 exactly match what the code outputs when no answer matches.
On Financial PhraseBank, 4 of 7 models fall below the 0.5948 majority floor under one rule and clear it under the other.
On three of four substring-scored tasks, no open-weight model was distinguishable from a degenerate predictor.
papers.takeaway: Published finance-AI leaderboard numbers may reflect answer parsing more than skill; the audit covers one benchmark suite.
